videos.title: President Donald Trump says US-Iran ceasefire is over, so what happens now? #BBCNews
videos.transcript: President Trump says the ceasefire is over. Iran says the memorandum of understanding has been violated. So what happens now? Well, technically there has been a ceasefire agreement between the US and Iran since early April, although both sides say that the other has violated it. And last month the US and Iran signed an agreement, anou that said that they would stop war on all fronts. Then earlier this week, three tankers were hit as they were trying to cross the straight of Hormuz. The US blamed Iran. They therefore reinstated oil sanctions on Iran. And last night, the US said that they attacked Iranian air defenses and anti-ship missiles. Iran responded saying that it attacked US military bases in Bahrain and Q8. But although Trump says the ceasefire is over, his negotiators are still talking. So, is this a negotiating tactic? And are we going to see an escalation with more attacks?
videos.summary: The video examines the breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire, which had been in place since early April. It outlines a series of recent events including an attack on oil tankers near the Strait of Hormuz, US oil sanctions, and military strikes by both sides. Despite Trump declaring the ceasefire over, US negotiators are reportedly still in talks with Iran.

videos.transcript: From the east coast to the Midwest, it is roasting in the US this Fourth of July weekend. Forecasted for temperatures between 100 and 115 degrees Fahrenheit. That's up to 46 C. It's already struggling to deal with the demand from data centers, and that sends power prices up. The largest regional grid in the US said real electric wholesale prices hit $1600 per megawatt hour at peak demand time on Monday evening, up from a more normal $40 earlier in the day. That encourages some electric operators to get more supply out of old oil and gas plants, and that makes the underlying problem worse. Scientists agree heat waves on this scale would be impossible without climate change from burning fossil fuels. Last week, Europe cooked in temperatures over 40° C. Germany estimates every day over 30 costs its economy €430 million euros. The heat keeps tourists at home, ruins farmers crops, and makes life hard for office workers in Northern Europe, where only about half of offices have aircom. Because until recently, there was no need for it. European cities are now realizing they'll have to spend millions on cooling public transport networks and urban spaces. Even companies that usually cash in on the hot weather have been finding the heat too much. Carlsburg told Reuters, "Beer sales usually go up with the temperature, but last week beer gardens emptied across Europe as drinkers just couldn't handle the

videos.transcript: Apple lost its challenge against landmark EU rules on Wednesday. The tech giant tried to refute the general court's designation of its app stores and operating system as gatekeepers. Apple is now subject to obligations aimed at giving rivals more room to compete. The EU digital markets act sets out a list of dos and don'ts for big tech with the threat of fines of as much as 10% of global annual turnover. It has triggered legal challenges by Apple, Meta, and Bite Dance since it took effect in May 2023. The ruling by the Luxembourg-based general court will strengthen the position of EU antitrust regulators. That's as they attempt to make space for rivals and give Europeans more choice. Apple first took its protests to the court in 2024. It again criticized the DMA on Wednesday, saying its mandate quote goes beyond what is lawful and proportionate. Apple can appeal on matters of law to the Court of Justice of the European Union, Europe's highest

videos.title: US extreme weather, Greece wildfires and US Pacific Islands brace for Super Typhoon | BBC News
videos.transcript: Get the latest now on the extreme weather conditions in the US. Authorities ordered an evacuation of the National Mall in Washington after a thunderstorms approach threatening the festivities there. Storms came amid a dangerous heatwave in Washington D.C. across most of the East Coast. On Saturday, nation's capital was reported to be among the top 1% of hottest places on Earth. Here's our weather presenter, Simon King. >> In the US, we saw that extreme heatwave, a big heat dome developing across the east of the United States. And temperatures in Washington D.C., in Philadelphia, New York, they were getting up into the high 30s of Celsius. But when you add in the humidity, it would have felt like 46° Celsius. So, really dangerous heat there. Now, what happens in when you get these situations with a big heatwave developing is that with a high humidity, that heat, it gives a lot of energy. Lots of moisture can go into the atmosphere. And you just need a trigger. And for the case of the US, we've had a a cold front moving its way southeastward across the US. And that brought the end to the stifling heat. But it ended with a big bang. So, you didn't just have the fireworks, of course, for the Independence Day celebrations, but the lightning, the thunderstorms were really quite severe across eastern areas of the US through yesterday evening and night. And through today, we'll continue to see some quite big thunderstorms moving their way southeastward across the east of the US. The heat will be more concentrated down towards Virginia, North and South Carolina. So, here temperatures once again getting up into the mid to high 30s. Whereas, it should start to feel a little bit more comfortable for the likes of New York and Washington and Philadelphia. Temperatures here should start to drop away in the coming days. >> And Simon, just how common are weather events like this there? >> Yeah, they are pretty common. I mean, the temperatures that we saw in some parts of the eastern states have been, you know, very high. In fact, record-breaking for some locations. Um and while obviously you don't tend to get records being broken every year, we know that with our changing climate that heat waves are becoming more intense. They are becoming hotter, more prolonged. So, you know, it it sets the scene to to see these sort of records being broken in parts of the US. But of course, heat waves aren't unusual in the US and it's not unusual either to see these big thunderstorms that develop um on the back of these heat waves. You know, uh so the US is well used to having uh severe weather like this. And of course, you know, tornadoes, we know they are formed by these big storms developing after a period of hot weather. Um and then, you know, some colder air coming in that can trigger things off to to bring those storms. >> Uh Simon, as we know, US not the only place experiencing uh these high temperatures, uh dangerous situations in parts of Europe, as well. >> Yeah, so in Greece, we've seen recently some wildfires. Now, again, wildfires in Greece, uh you know, aren't unusual. The the summer is becoming longer there because it's it's heating up, it's drying out. So, wildfires, you know, have been seen already so far this summer. And we've seen one recently that's affected uh some uh pretty big populated areas. So, um the concern there, of course, as we go through the rest of the summer is that we could still continue to have uh some wildfires with periods of heat building up. Um but elsewhere across Europe, well, again, we've got another heat wave on the way, the third of the year. So, like we saw at the end of June with record temperatures being set, uh temperatures will slowly rise again across France and into the United Kingdom. Uh here we're going to see temperatures getting up into the mid-30s by the time we get into the middle part of the week. And while this heat wave isn't likely to be as extreme, the temperatures won't be as high as we saw in June, it's likely actually this heat wave could last longer. So, forecasts at the moment suggest that the temperatures getting above 30° C across England for example could last for maybe 7 to even 10 consecutive days. >> Thanks to Simon there. Residents of the US Pacific territories of Guam and Northern Marianas have moved to emergency evacuation centers. This is all ahead of the arrival of a super typhoon due to make landfall on Monday. National weather service has described it as very dangerous as forecast a barrel through the territories with winds of 260 km an hour, rains and big waves as well.
videos.summary: This BBC News video covers a series of extreme weather events happening around the world. Weather presenter Simon King explains a dangerous heatwave and severe thunderstorms on the US East Coast, recent wildfires in Greece, and an approaching heatwave across Europe. The video also reports on a super typhoon threatening the US Pacific territories of Guam and the Northern Marianas.

videos.title: Apple hikes prices as memory chip costs skyrocket
videos.transcript: Apple is hiking prices as the cost of memory chips skyrockets. It's lowest priced laptop will jump from $599 to $699 with iPad prices also rising. For now at least, the iPhone is unaffected. Apple says it can no longer avoid passing on rising costs to consumers. The price of memory chips jumped by around 98% in the first quarter and has continued to soar ever since. That is driven by the boom in AI data centers. Companies like Nvidia have signed big deals with chip makers leaving consumer electronics firms scrambling to secure supplies. Apple said it had never seen component prices increase so much, so quickly. While iPhones weren't hit by Thursday's move, analysts say it's only a matter of time before they too face price increases. Apple shares fell almost 5% while Dell dropped 8%. Some industry watchers say Apple's rivals may have to do even bigger price increases as they lack the Mac makers deep ties to suppliers. Research firm IDC says the global smartphone and computer markets will both see sharp contractions this year due to the rising prices.
videos.summary: Apple has announced price increases on its laptops and iPads due to soaring memory chip costs. The price of memory chips has nearly doubled, driven by high demand from AI data centers, leaving consumer electronics companies competing for limited supplies. Analysts warn that iPhone prices may also rise in the near future, and the broader market for smartphones and computers is expected to shrink this year.

videos.title: How has Brexit changed Britain’s economy?  | The Economist
videos.transcript: How exactly has Brexit changed Britain's economy? It's been ten years since Britain decided to leave the European Union The dawn is breaking on an independent United Kingdom The country has been through six prime ministers since then and is now more divided, less influential and poorer than it otherwise might have been Brexit was a huge mistake Most economists agree that Brexit has damaged the economy Some say GDP per person is 8% lower, while others say it's only 2.5% We may not know the exact cost, but what we do know is that growth in most other big, rich countries has been faster than in Britain The effects are clearest in manufacturing Brexiteers promise to free Britain from the shackles of EU regulations They said that any trade losses with the EU would be more than made up for by greater trade with the rest of the world But that's not what's happened The value in real terms of goods traded with the EU has fallen by 7% since 2016 But trade with the rest of the world has also fallen by 6% Competition from China and high energy costs were already making life harder for British manufacturing But Brexit sped up its decline by introducing new barriers to trade with the EU, such as extra border checks and more paperwork Over 16,000 British businesses have given up exporting to the EU altogether— that's 14% of all exporters to the continent But it's not all doom and gloom Britain's exports of services have actually risen since 2016 by £62bn in the EU and £107bn in the rest of the world The biggest growth in output has been in industries with few trade barriers like IT services or advertising That has happened despite Brexit, not because of it Sectors where Brexit introduced new obstacles like financial services, they've done worse But Brexit alone can't be blamed for Britain's sluggish economy It fundamentally has the same strengths and the same weaknesses as before 2016— leaving the EU has just made everything a little bit harder
videos.summary: This video marks ten years since Britain voted to leave the European Union and examines how Brexit has affected the British economy. It looks at the impact on trade, manufacturing, and services, drawing on economic data to assess what has changed since 2016. While Brexit has made some things harder, the video also notes that Britain's economic weaknesses existed before the vote.

videos.title: South Korea unveils $576 billion AI chip investment
videos.transcript: South Korea rolled out sweeping chip and AI mega projects on Monday. >> President Lee Jang pledged investments worth more than $576 billion over several years. It's a move that aims to cement the nation's overwhelming industry leadership. Lee was joined for the announcement by the leaders of Samsung Electronics and SKH Highix. High bandwidth memory chips produced by both tech giants have become pivotal in the global race to build advanced AI systems. Lee said the world's two largest memory chip makers will invest around 518 billion with suppliers to build two new chip fabrication sites each in South Korea's southwest region. He announced plans for the southwest to host major chip production clusters drawing on abundant underused power. videos.title: Why is the UK not built for extreme heat? #Heatwave #UK #Weather #Climate #BBCNews
videos.transcript: Why is the UK just not built for extreme weather? We're just at the start of what's going to be an intense heat wave. But the reality is that the average summer temperature here is just about 16° C. With those mostly mild conditions, we're building for those conditions instead. But the future is going to be much hotter and much wetter. Large parts of our train network run on electricity and power lines sag in high temperatures. So that can mean trains get cancelled. We've also built our towns and cities with lots of rock and concrete. It absorbs the heat and then radiates it back out, making that heat even more unbearable. We're also building lots of shiny new apartments with lots of glass, which traps the heat, just like a greenhouse. And it may come as a surprise to those people not living here, but only about 5% of homes in the UK have air conditioning. All this means is that so far we haven't adapted our lives to extreme heat in the way many other countries already
